editions.title: Nscale loses Microsoft anchor as AI stocks wobble
editions.notification: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale's Essex data centre as AI infrastructure stocks slide. Here's what it means.
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the period is a setback for Nscale, the British AI infrastructure firm preparing a New York listing. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out as anchor tenant of its Loughton data centre in Essex, reportedly because grid officials said power would not arrive until the 2030s. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and is exploring alternative power. The timing is awkward: Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of its contracts, and the reported $35bn valuation now faces scrutiny. The report also lands in a broader cooling of AI infrastructure sentiment, with a separate report finding at least 47 AI infrastructure projects hit setbacks this year.

Markets are feeling the same nerves. Japanese stocks fell at the open as a chip-led tech selloff deepened on doubts about the AI trade, and a Korean pension fund reportedly lost about $137bn after Samsung and SK Hynix slid. Commentators expect Magnificent Seven earnings to test whether hyperscaler AI spending holds up. Chinese data showed growth of 4.5% in the third quarter, with AI-related exports offsetting weak domestic demand and a property slump, which gives Beijing room for support measures.

Elsewhere, Apple dominated the rumour mill: reports point to touchscreen MacBooks and an OLED iPad mini arriving around 6 November, and a robotic 360-degree HomeView display, though none of this is confirmed. Its new foldable iPhone Duo is in heavy demand, with walk-in stock reportedly unlikely on launch day. Google unveiled a Gemini 4 agent team that completed Minecraft autonomously, while Meta said a Claude-linked tool wrongly suspended a protest group's Instagram account.

Nscale says it remains committed and is seeking alternative power. The news lands just after its New York IPO filing, with Microsoft and Anthropic making up about 85% of contracts.

top_stories.title: Tech selloff deepens in Japan on AI doubts
top_stories.summary: Japanese stocks fell at the open as chip names led declines, with investors questioning the viability of the AI trade. The feed gave no index levels, but the move follows a weak week for AI infrastructure names. Magnificent Seven earnings are seen as the next test.

top_stories.title: Korean pension fund hit by $137bn loss
top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports South Korea's main pension fund lost 182 trillion won as Samsung and SK Hynix shares fell. The scale shows how dependent the fund is on its largest chipmakers. It underlines the market risk from the current chip slide.

top_stories.title: China's Q3 growth edges up to 4.5% on AI exports
top_stories.summary: China grew 4.5% in the third quarter, the bottom of its target range, with AI-related chip exports offsetting weak domestic spending. Property investment fell more than 20% in the first nine months. Beijing has announced support measures, giving policymakers room to act.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly shifts HBM base dies to TSMC 3nm
top_stories.summary: Seoul Economic Daily reports Nvidia asked Samsung, SK hynix and Micron to use TSMC 3nm for custom NVHBM base dies, with Samsung's foundry reportedly agreeing. The report cites better TSMC yields. None of the companies has confirmed it.

top_stories.title: Anthropic pitches Congress its own AI safety bill
top_stories.summary: POLITICO reports Anthropic has privately offered lawmakers a draft frontier AI bill allowing federal halts only for imminent, severe risks. It would give Commerce sole halt power and override some state laws. The move fuels debate over AI firms writing their own rules.

top_stories.title: UK watchdog proposes strategic status for Microsoft
top_stories.summary: The CMA proposes designating Microsoft with Strategic Market Status in business software, citing switching difficulty for around 20 million UK users. Possible remedies include changes to bundling, licensing and interoperability. Microsoft says its products are open and it will keep engaging.

in_brief.line: A London High Court judge reportedly threw out a £340m black cab driver lawsuit against Uber on limitation grounds.
Google researchers say four Gemini 4 agents completed Minecraft autonomously in 27 hours, at an estimated cost of $810 to $1,620.

Arm claims its AGI CPU offers about 2x modelled performance per rack against AMD's EPYC 9755 in agentic AI tests.
The General Conference on Weights and Measures voted to stop adding leap seconds to UTC, with the change coming into force next year.
Osaka electronics chain Joshin disclosed a cyberattack that has suspended some services, with a possible data leak not ruled out.
A critical Linux KVM guest-to-host escape, named PwnEscape, has been disclosed; patching is advised as fixes spread to distributions.
Reports say Apple stores in Bordeaux and Lille were looted during French protests that reportedly drew about 600,000 people.

editions.title: Nscale loses Microsoft anchor as AI infrastructure jitters deepen
editions.notification: Microsoft reportedly walks away from Nscale's Essex data centre weeks before its New York IPO.
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a setback for Nscale, the British AI infrastructure firm. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out as anchor tenant of its Loughton data centre in Essex, where grid power is reportedly not due until the 2030s. The news lands just after Nscale filed for a New York IPO under the ticker NSCL, with a float that could value it at up to $35bn. Microsoft and Anthropic make up about 85% of its contracts, so investors will watch delivery schedules closely. Nscale says it remains committed to Loughton and that its Microsoft relationship is strong. Microsoft has not commented.

The wider backdrop is a broad selloff in AI-linked shares. Japanese stocks fell as chip names led declines, Korean markets were hit hard, and South Korea's main pension fund reportedly lost about $137bn. Concern about whether AI spending will pay off also weighed on Oracle, Nvidia and neocloud peers. Analysts say Magnificent Seven earnings may test whether hyperscaler spending confidence holds. Meanwhile, the OpenAI Stargate project reportedly faces major obstacles, and Elon Musk again mocked the plan.

There are some firmer signals. Nvidia shares were set to end a three-day losing streak on a report that ByteDance and Tencent have each received H200 chips, and reports say Samsung and SK hynix may unveil a very large multi-year investment plan. Apple's iPhone Duo is dominating headlines, with supply strain, delayed shipping dates and a battery figure now confirmed, while Apple's AI features are reportedly set for China in December.

editions.title: Microsoft quits Nscale site as AI trade wobbles and iPhone Duo supply strains
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, weeks before Nscale's planned IPO of up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, and Microsoft has not commented. The report lands as investors grow wary of neocloud firms, and CoreWeave shares were marked down in coverage of the story.

The wider backdrop is a deepening selloff in US tech shares. Bloomberg reports that this is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI "picks and shovels" suppliers, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The FT also argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical constraints. Against that, SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data-centre moratoriums have delayed only a few projects so far. Meta's earnings, previewed by the FT as a test of confidence in AI spending, are the next major read-across.

Apple dominated the rest of the day's flow. The iPhone Duo, its first foldable, is reportedly sold out into January, with staff told walk-in buyers are unlikely to get stock on launch day, and Gurman calls the staggered pre-order rollout a "major mistake". Apple's EU energy label put the device's battery at 4,883 mAh. Rumours also point to a touchscreen MacBook and a HomeView smart display with a robotic arm, with a possible retail refresh on 6 November. Most of these remain unconfirmed.

editions.title: Microsoft Walks Away From Nscale Site as Neocloud Nerves Grow
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the day is Microsoft's reported withdrawal from an anchor deal for Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The Telegraph says Microsoft has pulled out weeks before the AI cloud startup's planned IPO, which is reported to seek up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. Grid connection delays at the site were also reported, and the story is being read as a sign of wider caution toward neocloud firms.

That caution fed into a broader theme of AI-trade nerves. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times, meanwhile, argues America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits of power, equipment and money. Investors will look to Meta's earnings next, which the FT frames as a test of whether confidence in the AI spending boom can be restored.

Elsewhere, Ericsson beat expectations with third-quarter adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn against a consensus of SEK 7.93bn, and its shares rose as much as 11% in Stockholm. On the chip front, a single unverified report says Nvidia wants Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, while a separate rumour suggests China could let major firms buy H200 chips under tight caps. Both remain unconfirmed.

Finance.title: AI trade unwinds as yields and oil bite markets
Finance.notification: Chip stocks endure their longest slide since 2008 as rising yields and $110 oil test the AI rally.
Finance.summary:
The dominant theme is a sharp unwinding of the AI trade. US chip stocks have closed lower for eight straight sessions, the longest run in years, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index has fallen about 16 percent. The selloff has spread to Asia's AI supply chain, with a Goldman Sachs basket of regional AI hardware names down 11 percent last week. Investors fear that higher borrowing costs could curb the data-centre spending that has powered the rally, and that financing strain at hyperscalers and neoclouds could reduce orders for chipmakers such as TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix. Some investors argue demand remains strong.

Rates and energy are compounding the pressure. Bond yields have been elevated, with the 10-year Treasury yield near 5.1 percent after a recent peak of 5.3 percent, while Brent crude has hovered around $108 a barrel. Hot September inflation has led traders to price a substantial chance of another Fed hike this year. Bank of America strategists warn that the cost of capital for hyperscalers has risen sharply, making AI investment harder to justify.

Elsewhere, markets are trying to steady. Futures rebounded after the Friday tech rout, and Asian and European indices were mixed to lower. Oil eased after Washington waived some Russia-related sanctions, and attention now turns to a busy week of earnings from Meta, Tesla and others, which will test whether the AI story is cracking or simply being repriced.

World.title: France's unrest deepens as government faces pressure
World.notification: Riots and looting across France push Paris into crisis talks, with calls for the interior minister to resign.
World.summary:
France dominates the world news picture today. Protests over living costs, fuel prices, school funding and public services turned violent over the weekend, with looting and arson reported in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Lille and Limoges. Reports cite more than 2,000 arrests, around 1,000 injured police officers and about 1,500 businesses ransacked. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is chairing a crisis cabinet, while politicians from left and right have called for Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez to resign. Macron has called for calm and order, and new protests are planned for 5 November.

The French stock index is down on the back of the unrest, and the 10-year French yield has eased, which points to nervousness about the country's public finances and political stability. Reports also note France now borrows at higher rates than Italy, so the political strain could weigh further on French assets if the government appears weak ahead of next year's presidential election.

Elsewhere, the energy complex is the main market theme. Iran has pressed Washington to accept a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with a seven-day ceasefire on the table, while Iranian officials hinted at a possible nuclear policy shift. Ukraine's strike of more than 1,000 drones on Russian oil sites, and Trump's decision to pause a Russia sanctions package, add to supply uncertainty. Oil futures have risen on these developments.

Tech.title: Nscale data centre setback; AI trade under scrutiny
Tech.notification: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale's Essex AI data centre as Nscale eyes a New York IPO.
Tech.summary:
The biggest story in tech today is the reported withdrawal of Microsoft from anchoring Nscale's Loughton data centre in Essex, according to the Telegraph. Grid officials reportedly said power would not arrive until the 2030s, and the project had already faced delays. The news lands just as Nscale has filed for a New York IPO under the ticker NSCL, which could value it at up to $35bn. Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of its contracts, so delivery schedules are now under scrutiny. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, but none of the companies has commented officially.

The wider backdrop is a shaky mood for AI infrastructure. Reports describe a weak week for neocloud stocks, and a roundup says businesses are trimming third-party AI software spending, with at least 47 AI infrastructure projects hit by setbacks in 2026. Markets are also nervous: Japanese chip stocks fell at the open on AI worries, Korea's main pension fund reported a large loss tied to a slide in Samsung and SK Hynix, and Bloomberg frames the Magnificent Seven earnings as a test of hyperscaler AI spending.

Elsewhere, Apple dominates the hardware agenda. Reports point to a touchscreen MacBook possibly arriving on 6 November, a 9-inch robotic HomeView display for 2027 or 2028, and launch-day supply problems for the iPhone Duo, which Mark Gurman calls a major mistake. In AI policy, Anthropic is reportedly pitching Congress a confidential frontier AI safety bill, and the UK competition regulator is proposing to designate Microsoft with strategic market status in business software.

Fashion.title: Paris Looting Hits Luxury Boutiques as Earnings Loom
Fashion.notification: Paris unrest hit Burberry, Louis Vuitton and Dior boutiques as luxury groups prepare third-quarter results.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story is the violence in France, where cost-of-living protests turned into looting in Paris and other cities. The Fédération du commerce et de la distribution estimates around 1,500 shops were affected, including luxury boutiques for Burberry, Louis Vuitton, Dior, Celine and Lacoste, while Sephora closed almost its entire French network. Retail executives and fashion bodies have called for government action, Macron has condemned the violence, and unions have called a nationwide strike day for 5 November.

The timing matters for the sector. Several luxury groups report third-quarter earnings this week, and France is a key market for LVMH and Hermès, so investors will be watching whether the disruption feeds into sales commentary. Shares of LVMH, Richemont and Kering were lower on the news.

Elsewhere, the business mood is mixed. Commentary pieces describe a difficult period for luxury, with weak numbers and empty chairs, and a possible loss of momentum in the United States, a major source of demand. Against that, Mulberry reported an 18% rise in first-half sales, and Chanel is preparing its first Wuhan store at SKP as luxury brands in China close weak stores and test new regions. Leadership change is also in focus, with open creative director roles at Calvin Klein and Alexander McQueen.
